newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks help to reduce competition case backlog.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks help to reduce competition case backlog.

text.p: The European Commission wants national competition bodies to help it work through a backlog of over 1,000 cases of alleged infringements of EU rules.

In a draft paper on cooperation between the Commission and competition authorities in the 15 European Union states, the EU executive proposes that work be shared in vetting restrictive practices, including cartels, and abuse of dominant positions.
Last year, the Commission took 433 decisions under the EU's two treaty articles regulating such activities.
But at the same time 559 new files were opened, lifting the total number of cases pending at the Commission to 1,178. It was the first time the backlog had increased since 1988.

Work in this field ranges from vetting requests for clearance of joint ventures that do not fall under fast-track merger rules, to cartel investigations and complaints of unfair of abuse of market power.

The Commission's cry for help comes as little surprise as European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has often said that some cases would be best dealt with at national level, leaving the EU to rule on issues with a more European dimension.
But it is unclear whether this will significantly relieve the Commission's powerful competition directorate general, of some of its workload in this active field.
This is because the Commission is ready to hand back only limited power due to doubts about national bodies' ability to carry out the work properly.
A draft notice published in the EU's Official Journal this week encourages firms to approach national competition authorities more frequently.
But it also states that the Commission would remain the sole power to grant exemptions under the EU treaty's article 85, covering anti-competitive practices.
This is an important part of the EU's anti-trust work as companies seek legal certainty for the agreements they make.

Recently, for example, the Commission exempted for 10 years an agreement by which Banque Nationale de Paris and Dresdner Bank cooperate globally in the capital markets and in financing international projects.

The Commission may also grant so-called block exemptions allowing entire sectors to be free of competition rules, either EU-wide, such as the exclusive distribution of cars, or nationally, such as the special tie between British brewers and pubs.

Competition lawyers said the German Federal Cartel Office -- which recently relaunched a campaign to strip the Commission of its competition powers altogether -- has been arguing for being able to grant exemptions, not just handle local complaints.
The problem is that not all EU states have brought their competition rules sufficiently close EU rules. Many simply do not even have a competition authority or one that works properly.
The notice is expected to be adopted formally later this year, but before the Commission is seeking comments from all interested parties, notably businesses which are primarily concerned.
